title: Binomial Theorem and Coefficient Extraction
quickIdea: (x+y)^n expands with binomial coefficients; a coefficient question is a counting question in disguise.
remember: (x+y)^n = sum over k of C(n,k) x^(n-k) y^k.
Coefficient of x^r in (1+x)^n is C(n,r).
Coefficient of x^r in (1-x)^(-n) is C(n+r-1, r) - the negative-binomial (stars and bars) form.
Factor out the smallest power before extracting a coefficient.

example.prompt: Coefficient of x^12 in (x^3 + x^4 + x^5 + ...)^3.
example.work: The expression is x^9 (1-x)^(-3), so we need the x^3 coefficient of (1-x)^(-3), which is C(3+3-1,3) = C(5,3).

gateAngle: This is GATE CS 2016 Set 1 Q.26 verbatim (answer 10). The same shift-and-extract move answers every generating-function coefficient question in the syllabus.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Coefficient of x^10 in (x^2 + x^3 + x^4 + ...)^4.
variations.why: Factor x^2 from each of the four brackets: x^8 (1-x)^(-4), so we need the x^2 coefficient of (1-x)^(-4), which is C(4+2-1, 2) = C(5,2) = 10. Cross-check by counting solutions of a+b+c+d = 10 with each part >= 2, i.e. a'+b'+c'+d' = 2: C(2+4-1, 2) = 10.

trap.what: Extracting the coefficient of the original power instead of the shifted one.
trap.why: After factoring x^9 out, the target power drops by 9. Extracting x^12 from (1-x)^(-3) gives C(14,12) = 91, which is wrong.
trap.counterexample: Coefficient of x^12 in (1-x)^(-3) is C(14,12) = 91; the correct answer to the GATE question is 10.
